title: Balliu et al. Conjecture (arc-disjoint linear branchings)
statement_text: In any strongly connected digraph, there exist arc-disjoint in-branching $T^{-}$ and out-branching $T^{+}$ (allowing arbitrary overlapping in terms of vertices), both with linear size and rooted at the same vertex $r$.
context_text: This conjecture was introduced in [2] to suggest that MRET (Maximum Reachability Edge Temporalisation) is in APX for strongly connected digraphs, since arc-disjoint linear branchings with the same root yield a quadratic number of temporally connected pairs. The present paper proves this conjecture by constructing a linear-size balanced bi-tree inside any strongly connected digraph.
attributed_to: Balliu, Brunelli, Crescenzi, Olivetti, and Viennot
paper_contribution: Proves the conjecture by showing that every strongly connected digraph on $n$ vertices contains arc-disjoint in- and out-branchings of linear size rooted at the same vertex, constructed via a balanced bi-tree of size at least $n/3$.
notes: Conjecture stated in prose in the introduction without a labelled theorem environment; attributed to reference [2] (Balliu et al., CoRR 2023).
paper_title: Temporalizing digraphs via linear-size balanced bi-trees

title: Problem 1
context_text: Digraphs may have 2-cycles; a digraph is strong (strongly connected) if every vertex has a directed path to every other, so it has $n^2$ connected couples $(x,y)$. Given a total order $<$ on the vertices, an arc $xy$ is forward if $x<y$, and a couple $(x,y)$ is a forward couple if there is a directed path from $x$ to $y$ using only forward arcs. With $t(D)$ the maximum number of forward couples over all orders, the ordered ratio $r_t$ is the infimum of $t(D)/n^2$ over strong digraphs $D$ on $n$ vertices as $n\to\infty$. The scheduled ratio $r_s$ is defined similarly by injectively assigning times to the arcs and counting couples joined by a path with increasing times (temporal paths); the authors show $r_t\le r_s$. An out-tree is an orientation of a tree in which a root reaches every vertex, an in-tree is the reverse; a bi-tree $T$ is obtained by identifying the roots of an in-tree $T^-$ and an out-tree $T^+$ that share no other vertex (every $x\in T^-$ reaches every $y\in T^+$), and it is balanced if $|T^+|=|T^-|$. The authors prove that every strong $n$-vertex digraph has a balanced bi-tree of size at least $n/3-1$, computable in $O(n^2)$ time, so both $T^-$ and $T^+$ have size about $n/6$; ordering the vertices along it gives at least $n^2/36$ forward couples, a $1/18$-approximation for the Forward Connected Pairs Problem (FCPP: find an order maximizing the number of forward couples), which is thus in APX (it is NP-hard, as it contains Hamilton path). Hence $r_t\ge1/36>0$, the central result of the paper; the exact values of $r_t$ and $r_s$ are asked for, and whether $r_t$ can be bounded below by an interesting function of $r_s$.
paper_title: Temporalizing digraphs via linear-size balanced bi-trees

title: Problem 2
statement_text: What is the maximum $c_{b}$ for which every strongly connected directed graph on $n$ vertices has a balanced bi-tree of size at least $c_{b}.n$?
context_text: Digraphs may have 2-cycles; a digraph is strong (strongly connected) if every vertex has a directed path to every other, so it has $n^2$ connected couples $(x,y)$. Given a total order $<$ on the vertices, an arc $xy$ is forward if $x<y$, and a couple $(x,y)$ is a forward couple if there is a directed path from $x$ to $y$ using only forward arcs. An out-tree is an orientation of a tree in which a root reaches every vertex, an in-tree is the reverse; a bi-tree $T$ is obtained by identifying the roots of an in-tree $T^-$ and an out-tree $T^+$ that share no other vertex (every $x\in T^-$ reaches every $y\in T^+$), and it is balanced if $|T^+|=|T^-|$. The authors prove that every strong $n$-vertex digraph has a balanced bi-tree of size at least $n/3-1$, computable in $O(n^2)$ time, so both $T^-$ and $T^+$ have size about $n/6$; ordering the vertices along it gives at least $n^2/36$ forward couples, a $1/18$-approximation for the Forward Connected Pairs Problem (FCPP: find an order maximizing the number of forward couples), which is thus in APX (it is NP-hard, as it contains Hamilton path). Here the size of a bi-tree is its number of vertices, so $c_b\ge1/3$. A construction of Balliu et al. gives strong digraphs in which every bi-tree has $|T^-|\le n/3+O(1)$ or $|T^+|\le n/3+O(1)$, leaving a factor $2$ gap. The authors also ask the analogous question for in-out-branchings, where the in- and out-branchings need only be arc-disjoint.

title: Problem 3
statement_text: Can we compute a left-maximal dfs-tree in $o(n^{2})$ time in minimally strongly connected digraphs? What about the complexity in the general case?
context_text: A digraph is strongly connected if every vertex reaches every other, and minimally strongly connected if every arc $xy$ is the unique directed $x$–$y$ path (such digraphs have at most $2n-2$ arcs). A depth-first search (dfs) tree of $D$ is a spanning out-tree $T$ (a root reaching all vertices) with a left-right order on the children of each node such that arcs of $D$ between disjoint subtrees of two children go from right to left. It is left-maximal if at every node the sizes of the child subtrees are non-increasing from left to right. The authors show that a left-maximal dfs tree rooted at any vertex reaching all others exists and can be computed in $O(n^2)$ time in minimally strongly connected digraphs (by repeatedly computing strongly connected components and out-section sizes); from it a balanced cyclic separator (a circuit $C$ with a partition $I,C,O$, no arc from $I$ to $O$, and $|I\cup C|,|C\cup O|\ge n/3$) is obtained in linear time, yielding a balanced bi-tree of linear size. Computing the left-maximal dfs tree is the bottleneck of their algorithm; they feel that a linear-time algorithm for the separator should be achievable, but computing a left-maximal dfs tree in linear time could be more challenging.
paper_title: Temporalizing digraphs via linear-size balanced bi-trees

title: Problem 4
statement_text: Is there a polytime constant approximation algorithm for RFCPP?
context_text: Digraphs may have 2-cycles; a digraph is strong (strongly connected) if every vertex has a directed path to every other, so it has $n^2$ connected couples $(x,y)$. Given a total order $<$ on the vertices, an arc $xy$ is forward if $x<y$, and a couple $(x,y)$ is a forward couple if there is a directed path from $x$ to $y$ using only forward arcs. In the Request Forward Connected Pairs Problem (RFCPP), the input is a strong digraph $D=(V,A)$ and a set $R\subseteq\binom{V}{2}$ of requested unordered pairs, and one seeks a vertex order maximizing the number of pairs $\{x,y\}\in R$ such that $(x,y)$ or $(y,x)$ is a forward couple; FCPP is the case $R=\binom{V}{2}$, which the authors show is in APX ($1/18$-approximation via balanced bi-trees). The paper shows that one cannot always satisfy a linear fraction of $R$: on the complete binary tree of height $n$ with each edge replaced by a 2-cycle (on $2^{n+1}-1$ vertices) there is a set of $n2^{n-1}$ requests of which at most $2^n$ can be realized, i.e. only a logarithmic ratio; the authors could not find instances where a $1/\log n$ ratio is impossible. The question of a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation (relative to the optimum) remains open.
paper_title: Temporalizing digraphs via linear-size balanced bi-trees

title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: Every strong digraph $D$ on $n$ vertices has a $O(\log n)$ size forward cover.
context_text: Digraphs may have 2-cycles; a digraph is strong (strongly connected) if every vertex has a directed path to every other, so it has $n^2$ connected couples $(x,y)$. Given a total order $<$ on the vertices, an arc $xy$ is forward if $x<y$, and a couple $(x,y)$ is a forward couple if there is a directed path from $x$ to $y$ using only forward arcs. A forward cover of $D$ is a set of vertex orders $\le_1,\dots,\le_k$ such that for every pair $\{x,y\}$ of vertices, $(x,y)$ or $(y,x)$ is a forward couple in some $\le_i$. The conjecture is motivated by the request version of the forward connected pairs problem: on the complete binary tree with every edge doubled into a 2-cycle, some request sets can only be satisfied in a logarithmic fraction by one order, yet $2n$ orders suffice to make every pair of leaves forward connected. It holds for bi-oriented graphs (undirected graphs with each edge replaced by two opposite arcs), by splitting a spanning tree at a centroid and recursing. The conjecture would imply that every RFCPP instance has an order satisfying a $1/O(\log n)$ fraction of the requests. A possible approach is to find $O(\log n)$ bi-trees (an in-tree and an out-tree glued at their roots) such that every pair has one vertex in the in-tree and the other in the out-tree of one of them.
paper_title: Temporalizing digraphs via linear-size balanced bi-trees
